name: Jupyter Foundation
summary: The Linux Foundation fund that pays for work on Project Jupyter. It controls money, not code: Jupyter’s own elected councils still make every technical decision.
intro: The Jupyter Foundation is a directed fund of the Linux Foundation, the LF’s 501(c)(6) trade association; Jupyter’s governance pages say its purpose is “to raise, budget and spend funds in support of Project Jupyter and its mission”. The LF announced it on November 19, 2024 at its Member Summit in Napa, California, with AWS, Bloomberg, Google and Meta as Premier members, Anaconda, Quansight and QuantStack as General members, and MD Anderson Cancer Center as an Associate member. It named the areas the money might go to: engineering, release management, community management, documentation and accessibility, and marketing and events. By October 2026 it had 25 members: seven Premier (AWS, Apple, Bloomberg, Google, Meta, Snowflake and Uber), eight General, among them Databricks, JetBrains and Posit, and ten Associate, mostly universities and research labs such as CERN and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

The fund sits beside the project, not above it. Project Jupyter itself is hosted by LF Charities, the LF’s 501(c)(3) charity, which it joined from NumFOCUS in October 2024 and which registers the Jupyter trademarks. Jupyter keeps its own governance: an elected Executive Council is “ultimately responsible for all dimensions of the Project”, and a Software Steering Council, with one elected member from each software subproject, coordinates technical decisions across them. The Executive Council’s members also sit on the foundation’s Governing Board, alongside one representative from each Premier member and one to three for the General members, so the people who run Jupyter help decide how its money is spent.

For someone choosing a technology, the badge says Jupyter has paying corporate backers and a neutral legal home, but not that they steer it. The foundation’s own site says joining “does not grant influence over the technical projects of Project Jupyter”, and an Executive Council member wrote in 2025 that it “doesn’t have any technical or strategic decision-making authority” over Jupyter’s subprojects. There are no maturity stages, and the foundation funds only Project Jupyter: JupyterLab, Jupyter Notebook, JupyterHub, the kernels and the rest of the subprojects.

sections.title: Who decides what
sections.intro: Four bodies share the work, as described in Jupyter’s governance documents and the foundation’s pages in October 2026.

rows.label: Executive Council
values: Elected leaders of Project Jupyter, set up in January 2023 to replace the founder-led model
Everything in the end: software, legal, finance, community and operations, mostly by delegating to the bodies below

rows.label: Software Steering Council
values: One elected representative from each software subproject’s council
Software decisions that affect several subprojects; each subproject runs its own day-to-day work

rows.label: Jupyter Foundation Governing Board
values: The Executive Council, one seat per Premier member and one to three seats for General members; chaired in 2026 by Rus Pandey of Apple
The foundation’s annual budget and changes to its charter

rows.label: LF Charities
values: The Linux Foundation’s 501(c)(3) charity and Jupyter’s parent organisation
Holds the project’s legal identity and registers the Jupyter trademarks

story: Project Jupyter grew out of IPython: the IPython Notebook appeared in 2011, and in 2014 its language-independent parts were spun off as Jupyter. Until 2024 NumFOCUS was its fiscal sponsor, and it was led by Fernando Pérez as benevolent dictator for life alongside a steering council. In January 2023 an elected Executive Council, with Pérez among its first members, and a Software Steering Council replaced that model.

In March 2024 the community was shown a proposal to move to the Linux Foundation, and on June 14, 2024 the Executive Council and the Software Steering Council approved it in a joint vote. The LF announced that LF Charities was hosting Jupyter on October 17, 2024, and Jupyter’s blog described the new Jupyter Foundation as “a vehicle for the project to formally engage with industry partners”. An Executive Council member later wrote that the council had asked the LF to set the fund up. It was formally launched on November 19, 2024 with eight members.

Membership has since roughly tripled. Apple, Snowflake and Uber joined as Premier members and Databricks, JetBrains and Posit as General members, and in 2026 Apple held the board’s chair and treasurer posts.

choices.choice: A fund beside the project, not a new home for it
choices.why: Jupyter already had elected councils that make technical decisions. Putting the money in a separate LF fund let companies pay for engineering and events without being able to buy influence over the code.

choices.choice: Seat the Executive Council on the board
choices.why: The project’s own leaders sit with the paying members, so they can tell the board what Jupyter needs and the budget follows the project’s priorities.
Jupyter’s leaders said the move would help sustain the project’s growth. LF Charities also offered a ready-made way to run a members’ fund next to the project.
